# The Nature and Quality of Waters

The human substance <note>The physical makeup of the human body.</note> is not compared in this way. This is the substance that helps to liquefy mixtures and to sublimate <note>term: Sublimation; the process of turning a solid or liquid into vapor through heat to purify it.</note>; water helps and reaches the veins through openings in the earth, through layers like fissures, and is filled by the mixture. In many cases, water is diversified not only in itself as water, but in the substances mixed with it and in its secondary qualities; it is said that spring waters are generally better than others. 

Yet this does not apply to all springs, but specifically to springs flowing over muddy ground; in the silt, however, a certain disposition is granted to each. It overcomes [impurities]. Or water that moves by itself, which, if it is not already "digested" <note>original: "digestiores"; meaning naturally processed or refined by movement.</note>, is purified lest it be spoiled by putrefaction. 

For that water which comes from muddy earth is better in itself. Not from every spring comes sand or mud; especially not from those which naturally possess golden properties. <margin>In another version, those things which are above are marked.</margin> Not every water flowing into gold-bearing channels is covered only by different winds. For this water acquires nobility from "coction" <note>term: Coction; a "cooking" or natural ripening of substances by the earth's heat.</note>. It is not just one thing, for it acquires a certain malice through various interactions, such as that in water which is not purified through depth and cooperation. 

Nor are all golden waters covered by different elements, but rather those that remain calm upon inspection. To heal the mouth <note>Possibly a reference to the health properties of drinking or rinsing with such water.</note>, water that has an improved quality and flows through is better. Mud actually cleanses the water and removes from it foreign and bitter things, whether it is strained in the channel or not, provided stones do not render it ineffective. 

Because mud is seen through which it passes... whether it be mud in a pool and nothing else. <margin>In another, sweet tastes were recently discussed, just as...</margin> For if this water was plentiful and strong, and contained gold, it would be mixed into its own purity by its volume; for the substance in the mud tends toward the sun, and toward the East, and in respect to its location, the water will be better. 

<margin>In another: a specific silence/tact.</margin> It is not so much that a great assertion will give them truth, but rather that which goes to the North. For water that tends toward the North <note>original: "arctos"; the constellation of the Bear, signifying the North.</note> from the South is bad, because the southern winds blow upon the vein <note>The "vein" or source of the water.</note>. And that which is said to descend... is better than the goodness of others. And that which is such that it is imagined to be sweet should remove the filth, so that it grows and dries into a pure state, as if it were from the white regions. 

Nevertheless, the reason for the heat <note>original: "calcis"; literally "lime," often used to signify heat or caustic properties.</note> in summer is that the flavor does not escape into the mud. There is no odor. The matter recedes from the hypochondria <note>term: Hypochondria; the upper part of the abdomen, then considered a site of digestion and vapors.</note> because in their action water is made, which is dissolved by that very action. It is noted through the mixture: cook something in two different waters...

...two of them, but let one be made wet by weight. Then quickly let the whole be weighed from the substance. That water which was lighter than all others was the better.

The water is combined, and thus the wise have testified that there is less resistance in its flow and speed of suction. <margin>In another, it is sublimated.</margin> And the physician predicts what he sends of his own: that the combined waters dissolve the subtle parts, and the spirit remains in the cooking so long as no benefit appears. For the spirit increases the likeness in the water. 

The ancients knew <margin><unclear>...which are...</unclear></margin> that water in its aqueous state exists as a fixed disposition of parts in thinness and thickness, if you please, which is simple. While the substances are higher, so that the heavy earthy parts can be separated from it; being held by the thickness, they are made to descend. And through the descent, they are separated from it, and the water remains purified and in its simple nature. 

And it will be that through liquefaction, homogeneity was separated and remained in it. We do not speak of this, because when water is separated from a mixture, or the parts are healthy in their own substance together, it is not very fitting that the substance and spirit which remain should be thus. 

For it is proper that water sublimate in its own nature, which removes the thickness of the cold and causes the mixture to descend. And this is how liquefaction exists: because the elemental part of the water is dismissed, and for a long time no thing descends from them that would be wondered at. For they are cooked there, and then many things descend. Much water is produced, which remains in a pure, very light clarity. 

And as for the descent, the cause is the shortness which is acquired over ten years. And indeed in a short time on the path, earthy things suddenly depart so that nothing else then causes residues to harden under the blood—things that would be wondered at! Moreover, that water is not raised up with such great praise...

### Chapter 4. On the showing of signs in those having human equality.

The signs and the gathered health which I have spoken of are the equality <note>term: equality (the "aequalis" or "balanced" state, considered the ideal healthy temperament where no single quality dominates)</note> of touch in heat and cold, and dryness and moisture; and the equality of color in a certain redness; and a medium figure of the limbs in quantity and manner, which are neither too large nor too thick. ### Chapter 7: On the signs by which it is known when any humor predominates.

**Signs that Blood predominates:**
The significations of a dominant humor are the same as the signs of repletion... and specifically, there is a heaviness in the temples and the eyes, and in the head and the limbs. A sluggishness of the intellect. Fatigue without previous labor. A sweet taste in the mouth. Ulcers on the tongue and perhaps throughout the mouth. A flow of blood occurs from other places, such as the nose and gums. This is also shown by... and dreams signify this, such as when a man in sleep sees red things, or much blood coming out of his mouth, or sees himself swimming in blood, or similar things.

**Signs of Phlegm:**
The signs of phlegm <note>Latin: *flegma*. The cold, moist humor associated with winter and lethargy.</note> are an excessive whiteness in color, softness, and sadness. A multitude of saliva which is viscous. A salty taste, especially in old age. Weakness of digestion, acid eructation <note>Acid reflux or "sour burps."</note>, and white urine. Much sleep and lethargy. Laxity of the limbs, fatness, and a light pulse that tends toward slowness and rarity. This is common in certain ages, regions, and arts. Dreams in which one sees water, rivers, snow, rain, and the like.

### Chapter 8: On the signs signifying treatment for obstruction

<margin>Sen.</margin>

**Section 18. First Chapter: Philaretus on the Univocal <note>original: *vniuocalib9*. In medieval logic and medicine, a "univocal" pulse refers to one that has a single, consistent character or follows a standard rule of definition.</note> Modes of the Pulse.**

The pulse is a movement of vivification <note>original: *uiuicatiōis*, meaning the process of bringing life or "vital spirit" to the body.</note> of the pulse of the receptacles of the spirit <note>original: *receptaculoz spū*. To the medieval physician, the arteries were "receptacles" that carried the vital spirit or pneuma from the heart.</note>, composed of diastole and systole, attending to the regulation of the patient’s spirit. First, however, that which is observed in the pulse is either univocal or particular, according to each specific condition. We, however, speak here of the univocal rules of the pulse. Particular pulses we have reserved for the discussion of specific illnesses in later sections. It is said, therefore, that every pulse is composed of two movements and two rests. For every pulse is composed of diastole <note>The expansion of the artery.</note> and systole <note>The contraction of the artery.</note>.

<margin>Knowledge of location</margin>

First, it is necessary to recognize all the internal movements that one may find. For it is impossible for one movement to occur without the other. Because of the space applied between them, the effect is thin [subtle]. Thus, my son, knowledge flows down. Because it is impossible to perceive the pulse as a whole, one part follows another so that the parts may be found: namely, two movements and two rests. The movement of elevation [expansion], the rest in that same state, the movement of depression [contraction], and the rest below until the next re-elevation. The movement of depression is hardly felt by the senses in most people. But according to others, this roundness <note>The physical sensation of the vessel under the fingers.</note> may be felt in a strong pulse, or in a great pulse during its elevation, or in a hard pulse after much restraint, or in a slow pulse because of the long duration of its movement. That is to say, it takes a long time for the depression to be resolved. Because of this, it is completed in a certain time. For when the greater part of the pulse has passed, it will be perceived as if one followed the other. And this is done as it is said: in many dispositions of the spirit, it is not perceived by the sense. The reason why it was established to touch the veins [arteries] of the arm is because the faculty is perceived there. And so that it is not resolved poorly, it should be done with rectitude [correctness], which is found in the rectitude of the heart and the three fingers that touch it. And it is required that the touch of the hand be on the side; for if the hand is extended flat in its width, the increase is felt. And with elevation, it causes a decrease, and they decrease in length. And the hand that is turned back [supinated] increases the elevation and length and decreases the width. It is also required that the touch be made at an hour when the pulse is removed from anger and joy and exercise and all passions, and from things that cause coldness, and from hunger.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic examination of the pulse, moving from the basic definitions of Philaretus to a more detailed classification of pulses based on their physical qualities and their mathematical relationship to musical harmony, citing Galen as a primary authority.</meta>

In summary, there are three species: the **soft** pulse, which returns to its proper state from a final compression; the **hard** pulse; and that which is considered **moderate** between them. Regarding these, there are species that remain above. **Full** pulses are those which fill the opening of the vessel, and for these, one must take care that they are purely evacuated <note>The author refers to "evacuation," likely meaning bloodletting or purging, to relieve the "fullness" or high pressure of the pulse.</note>. Because the clean pulse is moderate between them. And the genus that is above by its touch has three types: **hot**, **cold**, and **temperate**.

<margin>Note that the pulse is said to have the species which he mentions above.</margin>

A **frequent** pulse is one in which the perceived time between two pulsations is short; it is also called a "dense" or "thick" pulse. A **rare** pulse is one that is loose and resolved; between these is the moderate. The time consists of the **systole** <note>The contraction of the heart and arteries.</note>. If the contraction of the systoles was joined, there will be a time that pertains between all two **diastoles** <note>The expansion of the heart and arteries.</note>. If it was joined, it will be the two times of the two extremes.

The genus which is above according to quality and diversity is either **equal** or **divided** (that is, unequal). Another type is distinguished by the similarity or difference of the pulsations or the parts of a single pulse, or even one part of a pulse in five things: 
1. **Magnitude** or smallness.
2. **Strength** and weakness.
3. **Speed** and slowness.
4. **Density** and rarity.
5. **Hardness** or softness.

<margin>namely</margin>
<margin>The reason for a single pulse is that the parts of the diastole are faster.</margin>

Hence it is said that a single pulse is proportional to the end of its diastole through speed caused by heat, or is weaker through debility. And if you wish, you may expand the discourse: for it has equality and diversity in these mentioned genera and other parts. But according to the definition of strength reduced to both, an **absolutely equal** pulse is that which is equal in all these things. For if it were equal in only one of them, it is said to be equal in that alone; thus we say it is equal in magnitude or equal in speed. But the **divided** pulse is that which is not equal, either absolutely or in some specific thing.

<margin>as it is defined</margin>
<margin>And the reason of equality</margin>

The genus which is above based on order and mode of diversity has two species: **ordered diversity** and **disordered diversity**. The ordered is that which has a regular pattern of diversity... either ordered absolutely or according to a specific rhythm.

<column-break/>

...or ordered in such a way that it has two diversities. Thus, if there were an order or some other cause divided from it, it would be reduced to its own order so that it would be of one order. The disordered is that which is deficient. There are women <note>The Latin *mueres* is likely a transcription error for *modis* (modes) or *minores* (smaller), though "women" (mulieres) was sometimes used in gynecological pulse contexts. For just as the art of music is completed by the joining of sounds according to proportions <note>The medieval "Harmony of the Spheres" and Pythagorean theory suggested that the same mathematical ratios governing music also governed the health and "rhythm" of the human body.</note>, joined by their sweetness and gravity through intervals and the similarity of the times that exist between their pauses, so it is in the differences of the pulse. ### Second Summary: On returning to the urine and whether it should be believed. Chapter 1. On the indications of the discharge in urine.

**O**f the observations of urine, that which is sought is observed in four ways. First, that the urine to be considered be that very urine which is collected in the morning and remains for a long time—unless it is reserved from nature. It should not be that of one who drinks much water, nor should it occur when a bad thing or a restrictive drink is taken, such as water from a pipe <note>original: *aqua recita fistula*; perhaps referring to stagnant or lead-contaminated water</note>, because it changes the urine toward coldness and bitterness. And likewise, it changes bile, which by increasing changes the roundness and the [almun?] toward blackness. Also, things that change the urine according to their own color, so that things outside it might stain it, such as henna <note>original: *alchama*; used as a dye that could color the urine if ingested or handled</note>.
<margin>until</margin>
Since when someone is affected by an external stain, the urine becomes stained from it; it is not that the urine itself expels any humor, as when it expels bile or phlegm from itself by external movements or operations.
<margin>note</margin>
Among the dispositions that arise from the course of nature which change the color of urine are fasting, or wakefulness, or labor, or fear, or anger. All these things stain the urine with either sharpness or brightness. And it either makes the urine very thick, or no real restoration occurs, because these colors change those which ought to be in the urine. Similarly, they persist for many hours.
<margin>note</margin>
In which it is said that it should be considered for several hours, because its significance weakens and the color changes and the sediment <term>hypostasis</term> dissolves or changes or becomes thicker. Therefore, I say that the physician should collect the urine entirely

<column-break/>

into one <insert>wide</insert> vessel, lest any of it be lost, because the disposition there must be considered. It must be observed that the sun does not touch it, nor should it be shaken or chilled, so that the sediment <term>hypostasis</term> may settle and the significance be completed. It does not settle immediately when it is discharged, but in the vessel; nor should it be collected in a urinal that was not washed from other or previous urine.

### Chapter VIII: On the Urines of Different Ages

# The Practice of Health

<margin>In another version thus: so may your work and your assistance shine like clear water.</margin> ...aid, except through the science in which things are made for the completion of the world, and virtue, and the hope of knowledge, and action, and song. Just as a father helps us to demonstrate how health exists in common, or how that thing exists and is disposed, so this letter shows how it may be had by means of the science which we call Practice, which is operation and action. This is the part that tells us how it is to be built and governed. And as we have already completed the first and second parts regarding those things which are the means of the father <note>likely referring to the theoretical or "paternal" foundations of the science discussed in earlier chapters</note>, let us now be brought back into our study of the two parts that remained, concerning the practice itself.

Practice is divided into two parts: one is the rule of governing health <note>original: "sanitatem"; often transcribed in this manuscript's shorthand as "laitate"</note>, so that it remains in its integrity—this is called the "preservation of health." And the second part is the rule for governing the common sick, how to restore them to health; this is the "art of healing" <note>original: "medicandi"</note>. In this discourse, I will speak a compendium on the preservation of health, since the first things concerning our generation <note>the biological creation of a human</note> were two things. One is the sperm of the man, whose essence is hot and dry <note>original: "calida et sicca"</note>, according to the rule of the Creator; and the other is the sperm of the woman, which is moist. And because the nature of the woman is moist and cold, and the sperm of the woman has more moisture, and heat and coldness are surpassed in the sperm of the man, it is necessary that for the coagulation of these two seeds, there be a moist coagulation. Otherwise, the coldness and dryness would prevail in that which is made from them.

### Chapter 75
### On the regime of breastfeeding, and removal from the milk, and the weaning of the wet-nurse.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'O' in blue with red penwork filigree. The flourishes extend upwards and downwards between the columns and into the margin. The 'O' is the start of the word 'Oportunus'.</image-desc>

<margin>
What is required for the upbringing of children.
</margin>
The time for breastfeeding is suitable if, in the observation of the limbs, it is as much as possible like the milk of a healthy nurse. For a nurse should be chosen who is healthy, just as the mother was when she nourished the child in the womb. For they are the same in quality as the milk was. It is better not to take [other food] but to stick to the milk. The nurse should be checked to see if the nipples of her breasts are well-situated for nursing, which is very important. To avoid anything that might harm him, nursing twice a day should suffice. And should he not be breastfed too much? Yet let there be no harm from over-lactation. When he is back in his mother's company, it is better that a little honey be given to him before he is fed milk. Twice in the morning the milk should be expressed before the breast is given to him, especially if there is a "spot" <note>Likely referring to a discoloration or mastitis</note> in the milk. Bad, sharp, or sour milk will make the infant sick if taken on an empty stomach. After this, two things should be done as an aid to the child so that his disposition is made healthy: one is gentle motion <note>Rocking</note>, and the other is the sound of music <note>Lullabies</note>.

She should be protected from sadness, excessive passion, and other such things, for these corrupt the power of the milk. Perhaps she should even abstain from breastfeeding if she is troubled. For this reason, the ancients prohibited an infant from being nursed by a "stolid" <note>original: "stolidi" – meaning dull-witted or foolish</note> woman, lest the malice of her character be passed through the milk to the infant. Great care must be taken in this. Regarding the form of her breasts, one should observe that they are solid and large, but not sagging or loose in their size. In their texture, they should be mediocre in softness. As for the quantity of the milk, it is judged by its consistency and color.

<column-break/>

It should be consistent and not contain anything else, nor should it be "fistulated" <note>likely referring to sores or ducts</note>, nor thin, nor like whey. The taste should be sweet, not bitter or deprived of flavor. It must possess a liquid sweetness, not bitterness, nor saltiness, nor wateriness. It should be of a proper multitude and its parts should be similar. It should not be fluidly thin, nor too "cheesy" <note>original: "caseatum" – meaning thick or curdled</note>, nor should it show much foam. 

There is a test for this: when a drop of it is milked onto the fingernail, if it flows too freely, it is watery; if it stays fixed and leans longer without moving, it is thick. One can also test it in a small glass dish after birth, mixing it with the finger to see the quantity of wateriness and substance. The most praiseworthy milk is found where the wateriness and the substance are equal. 

If we find the milk to be harmful, we must change it through the nursing and the nurse’s diet. Regarding the nursing, if the milk is too thin, it has a bad odor. It is better not to give it until it has stayed in the breast for a time. If it is of a sharp heat, it should never be given while fasting. ### Chapter 4. On the regime of infants when they transition to the age of childhood.

<margin>In another: On the praise of all children to be found.</margin>
It is necessary that all care be given to improving the character of children and moderating 

<column-break/>

their behavior. In this regard, observe that no strong anger, love, or intense fear happens to them, nor sleeplessness, nor excessive thirst. Instead, always provide them with what they desire and crave. Do not permit them to be forced into anything they abhor; rather, show them the benefits of what is useful. One reason for this is so that the child grows properly in his habits and does not become a son of bad character. Another reason is for the body itself; for just as bad habits follow a bad "complexion" <note>the balance of the four humors</note> of the spirit, so too when bad habits become a custom, a "malice of the complexion" <note>a physical illness caused by humoral imbalance</note> follows them. For intense anger heats and dries the body excessively. And [fear] relaxes the vessels and inclines the complexion toward an excess of phlegm. In the meantime, while guarding their habits, if the child is agitated or afflicted in sleep, he should be bathed.

<margin>Form</margin>
The child should be allowed to bathe frequently. 
<margin>In another: he should not be dismissed.</margin>
He should be bathed abundantly, with as much water as possible poured over him, but care must be taken that it does not penetrate the ears. When he reaches six years of age, he should go to a teacher who may teach him with grace and order. He should not be forced to stay there constantly at first. When he reaches the age [of maturity], he should go to be bathed or washed more frequently, and this should be increased to keep him clean. If he is of a cold or moist complexion, he should be kept from fasting. And it is best to avoid heavy drinking in his beverages. The quality of the wine should be expected to provoke urine and move the bowels as he needs. When red bile is abundant, so that there is no provocation [of health], he needs to be satisfied with his food. If permitted, give him sweet, clear, cold water to drink. And this is the way to govern them until they reach fourteen years, with daily care for the moistening of their parts and the prevention of drying or hardening. They should be ordered in their habits so that they do not become weary, as is common in childhood and adolescence. Their character and mind change at this age. I have noted their regime, habits, and food. Afterward, we shall change to the matters necessary for adolescents...

### Chapter One of the Second Doctrine, of the Second Discourse: On the common regimen for adolescents and the virtuous. The main section on exercise.

Because the most important part of the regimen for the preservation of health is what follows—the preparation for sleeping and the regimen of rest—therefore we must begin our discourse with exercise. Let it be said, then, that exercise is a voluntary movement that makes the breath more frequent and deep, which is a necessity for the body. When a person makes a habit of it at the proper times and in a balanced way, they require no medicine. For those who neglect it, their nature falls into illnesses and the distress that follows them. This is because health is the remaining guide of the soul. We should know that health is maintained through a balance of nutrition. When nutrition is not appropriate—whether in its quantity or its balance—the light of health fades. None of the nutrients we consume are entirely transformed into the effective substance of the body; rather, in every digestion, some "superfluity" <note>waste or excess byproduct</note> remains. If this is not collected and expelled by nature, the collection of nutrients is not complete. Without doubt, the waste from digestion increases from that point. Through this "repression" <note>retention of waste</note>, the living humors will be weighed down and irritated. It produces a heaviness and a flow of matter throughout the body, and the limbs become sluggish. When this matter rots, it generates foulness and creates a "malice of the complexion" <note>an imbalance of the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>. If the quantity of these wastes multiplies, it leads to the aforementioned "repletion" <note>an overfilling of the body's vessels</note>. If they flow to any limb, they generate abscesses. These are not merely vapors, but are converted into complicated illnesses. Therefore, it is noted that these wastes must undoubtedly be collected and expelled. However, their evacuation is usually not complete unless it is done through medicines, which can be poisonous and undoubtedly break down one's nature. If these were not somewhat poisonous, they would not be able to drive out what nature wants to keep. Just as it is said of "purgatives" <note>original: "r̄yp̄aras," likely referring to cleansing drugs</note>, which purge and move the matter, they evacuate the superfluous humor by their bitterness. But they also weaken the strength of the principal organs.

<column-break/>

Exercise is the thing that most prevents the matter of repletion from congregating, provided that the animal regimens are suitable to it. It is that which renews the innate heat <note>the vital heat believed to drive digestion and life</note> and is brought about through use. It applies the natural heat to the body and purges the superfluities that dissolve daily. Movement helps move these "flatulences" <note>gases or internal vapors</note> and leads them to the places where they are usually expelled, so that waste does not accumulate every day. As we have said, exercise increases the innate heat, keeps the joints and sinews firm, and prevents obstructions from forming. For this reason, the limbs are made ready to receive nutrition because the waste products have been expelled from them. It moves the joints, softens the hardness of the limbs, and makes them light; it dilates the moisture of the vessels and the pores. Exercise also clears the pathways for the vital spirits to move through the limbs, which provides dexterity.

<margin>Rubbing <note>original: "Deitrio," likely referring to friction or massage</note>.</margin>

#### Chapter 2. On the second discourse: Some exercise is...

<image-desc>Initial letter "E" in blue and red with floral flourishes spanning the left margin of the second column.</image-desc>

Exercise is sometimes derived from the performance of certain activities; another is "pure exercise," which is what is intended here. Pure exercise differs in degree: some is heavy, some light; some is strong and vehement, some weak and gentle; some is fast, some slow. There is also "strenuous" exercise, which is a combination of strength and speed; and there is "relaxed" exercise. Between all these is the moderate kind. Species of exercise include wrestling <note>original: "lucta"</note>, and striking hand against hand, and pressing the jaws and ears, and twisting in various positions. Also, stretching with a bow, and jumping upward toward a thing from which one hangs, and jumping on one foot. Also, tilting with a lance, and managing horses. There is also the "standing" exercise, which is to stand on the tips of the toes with the arms extended in a swift motion. This is considered a noble exercise. For those who are weak or have low spirits, there is exercise done by being shaken while standing, or sitting, or lying down, or in a small boat in a tide, or sailing or fishing. For the strong, there is riding on horses and camels, or being carried in litters and wagons. Among the strongest exercises are those performed with heavy arms, or running a long course in a place...

### On the hour of taking exercise.

The hour that prepares the start of exercise should be when the stomach is clean. This occurs at times when the natural juices are processed and the "wild" <note>crude or undigested</note> parts of food are gone, so that the exercise may spread to the whole body. It is necessary that digestion should have already taken place from the foods eaten. One sign of this is the appearance of the urine, specifically its morning color, which serves as a mark of completed digestion. When it has been long enough, for sometimes a person remains un-nourished and "fire" <note>heat</note> is kindled in the urine, and the natural heat consumes the body if exercise is done then. It is not good for the stomach to be empty, but rather it should be nourished. In winter, the place should be warm, and in summer, it should be cool. It is better for exercise to be done when the body is full of good nutrients rather than when it is empty. And it is better for the body to be warm and dry, for then the quality of the nerves is improved. And when exercise is performed in all heat and dryness for the sake of battle, the body is led to health. When one has finished, he must remain quiet so that it may take effect, and the fluids may be expelled from the inner parts. Truly, all this should be preceded by rubbing <note>massage</note>, which invites the nature of the limbs to expand and dilate. And it is necessary that the rubbing be done with many hands. Then, one is anointed with oil according to the order, touching every limb.

<column-break/>

and this should be done with many and varied hands so that the friction reaches all parts of the body. Otherwise, let it be left so that another exercise may begin, either in time or for the belly. It is better that a person remains in his own house <note>to avoid exposure after exercise</note>. In winter, if one produces sweat, he should delay until it reaches the nostrils <note>meaning until the whole body has warmed and sweated</note>. But other prohibitions forbid this. In winter, the place must be warmed for a long time and heated temperately. Exercise should be used at the hour which is best. But as I have said regarding digestion and the expulsion of superfluities <term>superfluities: waste products or excess humors that the body needs to expel for health</term>, there are three things that are beneficial in exercise: one is heat, since in it health increases; second are movements, provided they are light; and third is the disposition of the limbs according to their expansion. When the sweating and the vaporous resolution of fluids have occurred, exercise should be diminished. When it has been diminished, one must return to the oil which makes one sweat, especially if the breath of those exercising is held. Since the day and the time of exercise are known to them, and by looking at the person, one knows how much he can tolerate. If the exercise is mild, it is done on the second day.

### Chapter 4: On Friction <note>massage</note>.

Rubbing is of different kinds: some is hard, which tightens; some is soft, which relaxes; some is much, which reduces the flesh; and some is little, which increases it. From these, nine combinations are formed. For rubbing which is rough <note>aspera</note>, such as with rough cloths, draws the blood quickly to the exterior parts. Another kind is gentle <note>lenis</note>, such as with the palm of the hand or gentle palms, which draws the blood inward. It also thickens a thin body, hardens what is soft, and softens what is hard. Furthermore, there is a type of rubbing performed before exercise, which is done when the desire to rise and move begins. Then there is the rubbing of reduction <note>recovery</note> which is done after exercise, which brings back the spirit and causes the resolution of fluids remaining in the limbs which were not evacuated during exercise, so that fatigue does not occur. This rubbing should be done softly and gently. The best kind is that which is done with oil.

### Chapter vi. On Washing

<margin>In another version: after it.</margin>
**T**hese things, whatever you find regarding cold water, are not [to be used] where the realm of the body flows back from every side, or when the age, the form, and the time are unsuitable. Do not use it during nausea, nor during vomiting, nor on a full stomach. Do not use it during wakefulness, nor when one has "rheumatisms" <note>an overflow of bodily fluids or phlegm</note>. Do not use it for a child or an elderly person. And it is common knowledge that for such a one, there is a light movement of the belly. Let this be done after washing with warm water until the body is made warm, so that the exterior parts may be made stronger; then he may retain his heat. If the desire was that it be used, the water should not be made very cold; rather, let it be more temperate. Let this be done after exercise, which is indeed a stimulation; before this, let it be done in the heat <note>original: "forno," likely a hot room or dry heat</note> where it is accustomed to be used. But anointing with oil is done in the manner it is accustomed to be used, and thus the exercise follows the massage and a temperate ointment, or perhaps a little faster than was customary. Then, after exercise, let him enter the cold water suddenly so that his limbs may be hardened <note>original: "durafiāt"</note> at the same time. This is perfected in a manner following the measure of his own lightness, and as much as he is able to endure, and before an obstruction <term>oppilation: a blockage of the body's pores or internal passages</term> comes upon him.
<margin>If he should enter for a drink.</margin>
Concerning when he has exited from it, let it be done as follows: let it receive an increase and then a decrease. And let the time of the return of the fluids to him be presided over; and the heat of it, if it was made swifter because the delay was temperate and modest; and if it was made slower because the delay was temperate, it was more than it ought to be. Likewise, let it be measured on another day, and whatever has been done from this, let the return of the color and heat be observed before he enters the water again.

<column-break/>

But in those things in which he wishes to act well, let the heat of the day precede the act, so that a certain quantity of heat may be perceived beforehand. And let him take care lest the belly be filled, and lest he be weighed down before everything else. He should not do this unless he has digested his food. Nor should he do this after vomiting or evacuation. Nor should he do this during a "colic passion" <note>severe abdominal pain</note>, nor during wakefulness, nor in any debility. In the exercise in which he is engaged, let it be strong according to the manner I have described. However, when washing with cold water according to the manners I have described, the heat is suddenly driven back to the internal parts. It prepares and strengthens him so that he may be stronger and more vigorous.

### Chapter vii. On the Regime of Diet

<margin>So that [it moves] to the limbs... rarely to be expelled.</margin>
**I**t is necessary that the health <note>here meaning the food or "wholesome substances"</note> which is eaten be preserved and protected, lest from it there be a medicinal nourishment like oil, juices, and the rest. For these, in their substance, are like blood-adhering things, and the reason is that they produce phlegm and govern the body. Or rather, let them be from such substances as are meats. These are the meats of suckling calves, and of yearling lambs, and especially those things purified from the outside which are gathered with healthy honey, so that no harm may occur. And use sweet roses suitable for the complexion, and wine with a light odor. But as for other things besides these, they are not to be used except in the manner of medication or for the preservation of health, being more like nutritious fruits. These are: figs, very ripe grapes, and dates in those regions where they are customary and where people are used to them. Truly, if a superfluity <note>excess of waste or humors</note> should occur in him, it must be evacuated quickly.
<margin>He shall have had.</margin>
Let him be prepared lest he eat anything unless out of necessity, or unless there is a desire or a bubbling <note>perhaps an appetite or "cooking" of humors</note>, and not unless he has been moistened by a decoction of Syrian herbs <note>original: "elix d s̄ianū," likely a medicinal syrup</note>. For enduring hunger is better than being filled with moist things.
<margin>...the harms of hunger.</margin>
In winter, besides the nutritious, let him eat sharp and hot food; in summer, cold food, or that which is of a lower degree of heat. Neither [extreme] heat nor [extreme] cold can be sustained to the point of excess. But you should know that there is nothing worse for health in a time of fertility than the hunger that follows a time of sterility <note>famine</note>.
<margin>But it should not be given in the time of hunger or sterility, but follows the time of fertility.</margin>
And so with this: if there is an internal or external burning, there are many for whom in the time of sterility it did harm; but afterwards, in the time of fertility, they were found to be filled with fluids and died. Thus, such a fullness is provoked, whether from the act of eating or from drink, because in whatever way they overfilled themselves, they were suffocated and died. In others, this happens by burning or by drinking some medicinal nourishment; it must be governed as they are digested.

Because it is so: take three parts of nuts <note>original: "nucum"; likely walnut shells or meats used in pharmacological prep</note> and one part of water. Therefore, let them be mixed and cooked until a fourth part is diminished. If for anyone an irritation happens from the preparation of wine <note>original: "mordicatio"; a stinging or biting sensation in the throat or stomach</note> through its malignancy, let him suck it up, and take cold water or a syrup in the morning and enter a bath. After which some bread is taken; know furthermore that mixed wine <note>wine diluted with water</note> inebriates more quickly. This is because the wateriness increases the ease of penetrating the spirit. One should never drink wine on an empty stomach <note>original: "ieiunus"</note> or before the limbs are imbued with water, or after strong motion, because these two cause more harm to the brain. Excessive drinking leads to spasms and madness, or sickness, or a hot head. Frequent drunkenness is a bad thing, because it fills and weakens the connections of the brain through its channels and leads to grave sickness, to apoplexy <note>original: "apoplexia"; a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, and to sudden death. Wine, furthermore, in many of the four dispositions <note>the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> turns into bad bile. In ten other states it turns into vinegar, and the harm from these is great. For some it is useful that once in a month it is taken until one is full, or twice, because it alleviates the bowels for some and brings rest, provokes urine and sweat, and resolves superfluities <note>excess humors</note>. But it is a greater harm to drink in the dark; wherefore no one having a weak brain should drink it, except in a small and mixed quantity. And for him who is filled with wine, it is better that he hasten to vomit if it be easy, and then drink much water alone or with honey, and after vomiting let him bathe frequently. Then let him be anointed much with oil and live. If it happens

This is because it refreshes the animal virtue <note>original: "animalis virtus"; in medieval medicine, the power of the soul that governs sensation and movement</note> which has been fatigued, and provides an immediate increase to the vital powers, making them strong once more. <gloss>This refers to the fact that man does not live by medicine alone</gloss> It also helps to recover the spirits <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle substances that carry life and sensation through the body</note> when sleep has provided a resolution of fatigue. Sleep, when taken as a precaution, tempers heat by moisturizing and warming <margin>note regarding the definition of sleep</margin> and it is a thing most beneficial to the elderly, because it restores moisture and sweetness to them. Regarding this, Galen said in his commentary that every night he would treat bile <note>original: "kolera"; yellow bile, one of the four humors</note> and sluggishness with aromatics to induce a midday sweat. And he said, "I am not fond of sleep, for I am not yet an old man," because he did not yet suffer from the excess moisture that makes one sleepy. Sleep is not something that reigns or conquers unless the spirit of the soul is first moistened, or after an abundance of food fills the organs. One should not pour too much hot water over the head, as it leads to a loss of vitality. A regimen of this kind is common in our medications. Healthy people, therefore, ought to consider their sleep so that it is taken at the appropriate time and in its proper hour, and not in excess, and they should beware of impediments. For sleep brings wakefulness to those who are burdened by reasons or powers! Sleep often forces one to wake many times and takes away rest. Because of the love of syncope <note>fainting or loss of consciousness</note> and the fall of virtue, the best sleep is that which follows the distribution of food. Similar sleep is that which comes after the food descends to the lower stomach. And for those who follow this strictly, it prevents bloating and rumbling, because sleeping on the back is hindered in many ways. In one way, sleep is diminished by instability and tossing from side to side. An impeding thing harms the sleeper with its own obstacle, which is why they should be accustomed to a delay in evacuation. Furthermore, to sleep specifically upon an empty stomach <margin>reason for the diminution [of sleep]</margin> is bad, and it weakens the vital powers. Likewise, to sleep upon a full stomach before the food has reached the stomach's curves is bad, because deep sleep comes with tossing from side to side. Since the soul is troubled by that which normally disturbs it, sleep resulting from poor digestion leads to heavy breathing and disturbances, and it brings on a state of stupor and corrupts the digestion.

### **Chapter 17: On Fatigue**
*The species of fatigue that follow exercise...*

It is permitted for anyone who adds massage to their routine. The types of things that happen are two; or rather, there are three species: ulcerous, stretching, and inflammatory <note>original: "ulcerosa, extensiva, et apostemosa"</note>. The first that is added is the fatigue which is called friction and drying. The "ulcerous" is that fatigue which comes from such a cause that, moreover, without the body being quiet, a likeness of ulcers is felt through the depth of the senses and the depths of the body itself. This is felt when the area is touched. And it is measured in its own movement. One feels it like the pricking of thorns <note>original: "spinatum punctura"</note>, and movement is dreaded so much that it torments the side and is stretched with weakness. And the congestion <note>original: "oppilatio"; a blockage of the bodily "pores" or channels</note> becomes more acute. From this increase, tremors and fevers occur. This itself is a multitude of superfluities in the vessels and the limbs, which is a liquefaction of the flesh and the fat due to strong movement.

<margin>natural entities</margin>

<column-break/>

And finally, these are bad humors <note>original: "humores mali"; the fluids of the body when they become unbalanced or "corrupt"</note> which, if they rush through the body, corrupt the blood. Therefore, if the damage is diminished quickly, the harm will be less. For much evil can occur when this kind of fatigue happens. And because it arises from the first movement, congestion occurs, and as movements increase, the acute humors are separated from these, and they remain in the nourishment, and sometimes even in the flesh. And because of the hard vessels <margin>or "durable"</margin> the person feels his body as if it is being rubbed, and feels heat and stretching, and dreads movement to the point that he dreads lying on his back in the place where the labor was. This comes from the remaining superfluities. For this has existed without a doubt. Now, the stinging <note>original: "mordicatio"; a biting or gnawing sensation</note> or the acidity of the vessels exists. Between these, a corruption exists with the loss of quietness. Therefore, it often happens that the pain is not complete. One type is when completion happens through sleep; another is where there is a diversity that produces pain and takes away rest. Moreover, it is in the muscle and the fibers <note>original: "villum"; refers to the grain or fibers of the muscle</note>, which are drawn into a thinness. But inflammatory fatigue <note>original: "apostemosa lassitudo"</note> is when heat is released in the heart, and it is swollen, similar in its magnitude and color. And it happens that when it is touched, it moves and is felt as an extraction. But "detentive" or "rarefied" fatigue is that which is felt in the body as if the limb were being dried out. And it is superfluous. And this happens either from much exercise with little food, or <margin>or "blindness" through hardness</margin> from the application of heat. And because it happens from the thinness of the air and from the diminution of the mind <margin>or "land of alum"</margin> and from much fasting. The ways in which fatigue happens are two. The first is above. For fatigue either happens because of exercise—and this is more secure when it has a method of healing as mentioned before—or it happens of itself. This is the precursor to every sickness, the medicine for which has the same method as before. Or it is joined with another, having its own material causes, either by themselves or through another. And when you move the rule of simple powers toward the rule of the limbs, you will follow the rule which I have given. And this is the principal concern: to have a greater care for that which is more established in ruling the body. And because of this, massage should be performed. Massage is performed for three reasons: either for strength, for nobility <note>likely referring to the restoration of the "noble" organs like the heart or liver</note>, or for the sake of the massage itself. ## Chapter 17. On Other Robust Faculties.

It is permitted to speak of the superfluities <note>original: "superfluitates"; waste products of digestion and metabolism according to Galenic medicine</note> which operate within the small vessels, and because of this, much happens during sleep. When those humors are overly abundant, a blockage <term>oppilatio|a clogging or obstruction of the internal passages or pores</term> occurs in the arteries, and when they become too dry, it will cause a fever. This swelling is of the sort that happens in the jawbones and the twisted vessels. In a healthy person, this happens without cause and when it is excessive, it is an evil thing; yet, it is better if it comes out. This is the kind of discharge that follows digestion, as it is the expulsion of superfluities. Among some, these obstructions cause a chill from acute vapors, little resolution of the spirit, and a putrefaction from sleep before it is completed. The expulsion should be comprehensive. To find the middle way, one must look to other robust healings, as found in other philosophers <note>original: "philosophis"; likely referring to medical authorities like Galen or Avicenna</note>.

## Chapter 18. On the Medicine for Fatigue Arising from Intense Study.

Next, we consider when fatigue <term>lassitudo|a state of physical or mental exhaustion or "weariness"</term> comes upon a person through intense study, a matter of medicine and many anxieties from which fevers arise. Or when an ulcerous fatigue appears from excessive movement, it is a serious matter. And when there is a multitude of humors, they should be expelled, for they bring about a loathing of food. He warned that this should be done while the person is hungry and through evacuation. The resolution should be gentle, directed to the part where there is much coldness, using oil that is not tainted. And on the second day of recovery, let a restorative exercise be encouraged; on the second day, let them be evacuated in quality but diminished in quantity. On the second day, they should be nourished with moistening things. If it is a young person, and there is raw phlegm in the fat of the intestines, let there be friction <term>fricatio|therapeutic massage or rubbing</term>, for it matures the humor and, through the medium of heating, penetrates the nature of the fat. For this, oil of a warming nature is very beneficial.

### Chapter 15. On other conditions that follow from these.

Before we speak of the remaining matters, in these conditions, we shall turn to managing the fatigue <term>lassitudinem|weariness or physical exhaustion</term> which comes from external causes, such as the thinness of the air or excessive rubbing and bathing. In the first case, dry rubbing is medicinally helpful, followed by rubbing with oil. Another cause is the thickness <note>original: "spissitudo"</note> which comes from

<column-break/>

<margin>Note: regarding the winter season.</margin>
<margin>Note: he sits in a dusty place.</margin>
<margin>Note: the upper part for a man who has an external rupture.</margin>

coldness, or from remaining in a dusty place, or from a multitude of superfluities, or from their thickness or viscosity <term>viscositate|a sticky or thick consistency of the humors</term>. From this, it happens that the breath is retained or a thickness from old matters emerges from the depths; this will not be delayed by the preceding causes, or because the place was dusty or the rubbing was too harsh. Those whose condition comes from coldness are pale in color, slow to warm up, and their sweat and response to redness is slow. These people must be moistened in hot baths, and they should be turned over on a cloth of equal heat until they sweat, so that their heavy limbs are resolved by the warm, medicinal oils. Those who come to the bath from exhaustion, if they have these signs, must be treated by expulsion of the superfluities; the regime should assist and resolve this through the bath and the application of ointments. Those who travel and are covered in dust or have been rubbed harshly should come to the bath with an application of oils. Before this, they should use a soft rubbing both before and after the bath. There are those for whom weakness happens from excessive exhaustion with little rubbing, or it happens from excessive sexual intercourse <note>original: "coitu"</note> or frequent bathing. These must be treated with care and a lighter dry rubbing, which is then assisted with aromatic oil, and they should be given moistening nourishment in a moderate quantity—neither too hot nor too cold. This is especially true if weakness, or wakefulness, or restlessness occurs, or if dryness happens in youth. This is even more necessary if there is a failure of digestion or if the food is not sufficient. Furthermore, if this happens from an excess of bathing and a multitude of eating and drinking, it must be purged, or if there is excessive moisture in the tongue so that it harms the perceptions. Such a person will be healed by specific medication for that part. And if it was from any of those things that are contrary to nature, such as too much cold or too much moisture from the bath, he should be instructed to use harsh and dry exercise and rubbing without oil, or rubbing with very little oil.

### Concerning the medicine for exhaustion from evacuation. Chapter 16.

This type of exhaustion, which arises from evacuation <note>original: "pte uacā" (parte vacante); likely referring to exhaustion following bloodletting, purging, or excessive exercise</note>, is recognized by determining whether the efficient cause is within the veins or outside the veins. If it is within the veins, it is revealed by the stench of the urine and by the disturbances of the nutritional processes. This often occurs due to the abundance of female superfluities <note>original: "muliarudo iueis"; likely referring to menstrual cycles or related humors</note> generated within the veins, or because of their lightness and the speed with which the body's nature expels them. It is also seen in the condition of the urine, whether it appears clear or turbid. If these signs appear, it indicates that the issue has exited through the veins. If not, then the cause is external. If the exhaustion is from superfluities, you should cleanse the interior of the veins. It will also suffice to increase the restorative regimen that we mentioned regarding the shoulder-blade <note>original: "icapula rose"; likely a specific therapeutic area</note>, which is triggered during exercise. If another division occurs among the thoughts, strive to evacuate them; first, make the patient rest and sleep. When his vigor returns, let him be anointed with oil and warm water, if he can tolerate the bath, following the procedures we have described. Let his diet be changed from what we said: let his drink be light, made from common grain to strengthen him, and let there be a nutritional viscosity in it, such as barley or spelt. From the meat of birds, let there be syrups, specifically oxymel <term>sirup acettosus d̃ melle|a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> and hydromel <term>y dromel|a mixture of honey and water</term>, as well as white bread. Do not prohibit any of these things, for they are more mature and beneficial. However, avoid giving him heavy bread; let him move toward white, refined bread. This regimen will assist him. Above all, ensure evacuation.

### Chapter 17. Concerning the regimen of bodies whose constitutions are not good.

These constitutions <note>original: "complexio"; the unique balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in an individual</note> are either those in which a bad state is increasing <margin>Or: good.</margin> or those which come from external causes. Natural constitutions are innate; <margin>Or: good.</margin> these bad constitutions are found in those who have long persisted in errors of regimen. Others are in a state of bad constitution from the root <margin>Or: beginning.</margin> <note>meaning they were born with it</note>. For those who suffer errors from birth and have a delicate nature, these may perhaps be corrected through a specific physical discipline. They are in a poor state due to the dispositions of their own body or the composition of their members, which is why they are called "old" by the wise.

## Chapter 1. Concerning the dietary practices, which is a universal summary.

The summary of the rule for governing the elderly... The common goal is that they should be warmed and moistened. This is achieved through nutrients, baths, <note>the text likely refers to 'wine' or 'water' here</note> and plenty of sleep. They should spend much time in bed, more than the young. To soothe their weariness, one should provoke the expulsion of phlegm <note>one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture</note> from their pathways. Their diet should be light and easily digested. Use massage for the body with oil until it glows. Then comes riding, or if they are too weak for riding, let them be carried. For those who are extremely weak, they should be massaged once or twice. Afterward, something sweet-smelling from aromatics should be applied to the heart. Because of the cold [of old age], they should be warmed. If they wish, let them be anointed with oil, for this is of great benefit to the animal spirit. <margin>Or: balsam oil.</margin>

## Chapter 2. Concerning the nourishment of the elderly.

First, the elderly must be fed little by little. They should be nourished twice a day in small amounts, according to their digestion and strength, <margin>In the beginning.</margin> or their weakness. At the second hour, let them eat bread well-rubbed with honey, and at the third hour after their bath...

# Chapter 6. On the exercise of the elderly.

The true revitalization of the elderly depends on the diversity of their bodily disposition. One must consider whether they suffer from illnesses or are unaccustomed to exertion. For just as their health was maintained by balance in their prime, so should their exercise be temperate. And if one limb is in better condition than another, let that part be exercised differently. Furthermore, if someone suffers from heaviness in the head, or experiences "images" <note>hallucinations or visual disturbances</note> or epilepsy, or matter descending to the neck, or frequent vapors rising to the head, exercise that shakes or tilts the head is not beneficial. Instead, the mode of exercise ought to be directed downward to relieve what has accumulated. If the exercise is intended to clear the lower parts—
<margin>That is, for the purpose of extraction.</margin>
and if the ailment is in the feet, it is best to use movements of the upper body, such as moving the hands
<margin>That is, moved according to [the prescribed] measure.</margin>
as if throwing stones or lifting weights. And if the ailment is in the middle of the body, such as in the
<margin>Oh, if only a comparison were present here!</margin>
spleen, the liver, or the twisting of the intestines, such exercises should be given while fasting, unless there is something to prohibit it. But if the ailment is in the region of the chest, exercise of the lower body would be harmful. And if it is in the kidneys or the sacrum, upper-body exercise is not helpful. For in these cases, exercise should not be ordered simply to make the parts stronger, as is done for other ages. Indeed, for elderly servants, the type of exertion that benefits them is different from what benefits other old men. Therefore, weak limbs should be made stronger in an orderly fashion, following a method of exercise that 

<column-break/>

is suitable for them and the condition of their limbs, so that they are not harmed. For any [excess] is harmful, whether it be too much heat or dryness, or if the matter is inclined toward putrefaction <note>the breakdown of humors leading to infection or fever</note>.
<margin>Or: those fearing lest it should putrefy.</margin>
Then, maturation must be encouraged in them. Truly, this is the way the regimen of the body and its composition is made suitable. And there were also these chapters: The first chapter
<margin>Or: sharply.</margin>
on the teaching of certain things, from the third discourse: On the regimen for those who suffer from an excess of the hot complexion <note>the "complexion" refers to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> or heat.

When a living being is passive, and the factors that increase heat are equal and continuous, then there is no such excess, for then it lacks nothing. But when heat exists alongside
<margin>Note</margin>
dryness, it is possible for this state to persist for a long time. 
<margin>Note</margin>
Heat cannot long endure in company with moisture, because when moisture overcomes heat, it extinguishes it. Likewise, when heat overcomes moisture, it dries it out—this is the disposition and balance
<margin>Or: thus if moisture overcomes this, then it dries this, and so it is diminished.</margin>
of the complexion. Therefore, it is better for moisture to prevail, which happens in the fullness of youth. But as one descends into old age, moisture [of a healthy kind] decreases and the signs of old age increase, while heat diminishes. This is to say that the highest rule of governing the complexion is gathered from two things: one is to reduce the body to balance according to one's will, and the other is to sustain it through whatever calamity exists. First, we consider moisture; 
<margin>Only humor.</margin>
ordinarily, most people tolerate it as long as it is ordered toward balance. For in the beginning, a well-ordered regimen brings their heart to equality. But thirdly, it is possible, if their regimen is followed correctly, that there will be patience and full relief from the ailments found in them. Because whether the composition is moist or hot, if they are tempered in these two passive qualities, first their vigor will be maintained, and it will make their complexion temperate. They will be quick in their movements and swift in their gait. But as the years pass, the heat will decrease and the dryness will increase, until their complexion is called "dry." In many, this generates much red choler <note>original: "cola rubra"; red bile</note>. Therefore, their regimen ought to change with their age, just as the rule of nature changes; they must change their regimen to that which balances the loss of heat.

# Chapter 2. On the ventilation of the temperament in which there is coldness.

Here is how this matter stands: when there is an increase [in coldness], in those whose exercise is passive, they must be relieved when the heat proceeds according to the increase with hot [remedies] between moisture and dryness,

<column-break/>

lukewarm and sharp and warming, and other great evacuations of the humors, through previous wounds that cause flow and exhaustion in those living with them. Some have a temperate moisture, yet it happens to them that the moisture within them creates a density. For those in whom this density reigns, the regimen should be the same as the regimen for the elderly.

# Chapter 3. On the regimen of water.

## Chapter 8. On the regimen for those sailing at sea.

For those suffering at sea, dizziness <note>original: "vertigo"</note> and a "turning of the spirit" <note>original: "revolutio anime"; refers to the sensation of the stomach turning or fainting</note> frequently occur. The spirit is moved by nausea and vomiting. This happens especially during the first days, but afterward it settles and rests. One should not forcefully restrain the nausea and vomiting at first, but let it proceed until the digestion <note>original: "pipis/pepsi"</note> is cleansed. However, if it becomes excessive, it should be restrained. If it happens that the vomiting is harmful, it is good to eat fruits such as quinces <note>original: "atonia/cidonia"</note>, citrus fruits, and pomegranates. Finally, if smallage <note>original: "apya/apium"; wild celery</note> is drunk, it will prevent nausea from being stirred up and will also settle the spirit. Wormwood <note>original: "absinthium"</note> and other bitter things are prohibited, as are sour things which draw the vapors of the water to the head; these should be forbidden to the sailors. Also, foods such as lentils and those that are easy to digest are good. Use a little calamint <note>an aromatic herb related to mint</note> and avoid the spray. A pure spirit in a well-ventilated place...

### Chapter 3: On Evacuations
<margin>note</margin>
**Know** that it is sometimes necessary to evacuate <note>original: "evacuare"; to purge the body of excess humors through bleeding, sweating, or laxatives</note>. This shows the rectification of medications. 
<margin>note</margin>
Whether it be from an accident, fullness, or from the complexion in governing actions. Thus, if it happens that nature wishes to loosen the bowels, then a true loosening follows. ### Chapter XI. On vomiting...

Without number, however, as physicians make them vomit easily, or through the [treatment] of people who have such [conditions] and who breathe poorly, and who are fit for spitting blood. And people having **choler** <note>original: "colla"; yellow bile</note> in their throats, and those who are able to [clear] their throats from the foulness that prevails. In a body with weak health, and those who are very fat, for the virtue is [weakened] unless the belly is loosened. In such matters, it is better to vomit the bile... or through use, those for whom it is difficult to vomit should have a custom of vomiting. For if these [patients] have been proven for vomiting, they will not be restrained by the force of the vomiting... who [direct] the bile and the belly into the limbs... more faithfully... to the parts of health... there are other things which are unpleasant to vomit... they should be expended easily.

### Chapter XIII. On what the sick person ought to do

When he who has vomited has escaped from his vomit, he should refresh his mouth by washing it with vinegar and warm water so that the heaviness it brings to the head may be removed. And he should chew <term>mastic</term><note>A resin from the mastic tree used for dental hygiene and to settle the stomach.</note> and drink syrup of marshmallows. Let him beware if he immediately takes food and drink. After he eats, unless he is in ointments and powders, he should be washed quickly and then go out. And if it is necessary to give him food, let it be something like a boiled capon which is good and quick for digestion.

### Chapter XIV. On the benefits of vomiting.

Vomiting should be done once or twice a year, as in the second year it was difficult on that day... and so that what has arrived at the stomach might be expelled. For it acts through a certain facility that is preserved with it; otherwise, it is more of an evil. For it does not have anything to nurture it, just as in the bladder there is red bile which descends to it, but it removes the heaviness that it brings to the head and clears the vision. It also takes away loathing of food and benefits the stomach.

### Chapter XIV. On the Nature [of Dangers]

Superfluous vomiting is harmful. For excessive vomiting hurts the stomach and weakens and dissolves it. It makes it prone to the arrival of harmful matter. Therefore, it is necessary to be cautious in its use. It brings on headaches and pains, especially those that are from the satiety of the stomach. It also acts as a harm for epilepsy and causes the wasting of the limbs. The superfluity of it is unclean and harms the lungs and the eyes, and sometimes a vein may burst. From these things, it is clear that one should not fill the neck with it. Indeed, it leads to a loss of moisture. And this action produces bad and destructive diseases, such as the fullness of the <term>phlegm</term><note>original: "phileduis"; likely "phlegmatis".</note>, and it hinders food and drink.

# Chapter 17. On the Enema.
<margin>In another [text] it is called a "sanzan."</margin>
The **Enema** is a noble medicine for expelling superfluities <note>Excessive or corrupt humors that caused disease.</note> that are in the intestines. It is used for pains in the kidneys and bladder, and for those who suffer from <term>colic</term><note>Severe abdominal pain caused by gas or obstruction.</note>. By its power, it eases the superfluities of the <term>liver</term><note>original: "epur"; the liver was seen as the site of blood production.</note>. When these things are trapped, they weaken the liver and lead to fever. From enemas, a clearing is made by expelling the remaining matters which they leave in the bowels. Regarding the form of the tube, as was said in the chapter on colic, the better it is made, the better it reaches the upper parts. Then let him turn himself to the side that hurts... it is better, however, to use warm rubs, which help to increase the flow and stop nausea. A bath is often used to make the humors "boil" and be purged. The purpose of these things is to release the air and humors that are held back. And for this reason, if you first use a bath, follow it with the enema. And if there are <term>pustules</term><note>Sores or ulcers.</note> in the intestine, or fever, or other ailments, do not let the enema remain too long in the anus, lest it cause harm by being used incautiously.

# Chapter 18. On Epithems.
**Epithems** <note>original: "Epythemata"; topical applications of liquid or poultices to the skin over a specific organ.</note> are named for the local places where the sickness reaches. And they perhaps have two powers: one that is soothing and another

<column-break/>

that is <term>astringent</term><note>original: "ingellanū"; having a tightening or drying effect.</note>. There is a greater necessity for soothing than for tightening. When the application is made during the time of soothing, it will prevent the disease from taking hold. These are used when the body is weak, such as using fractured barley to make an emplaster over the sores. Plasters are similar to epithems, but plasters are hard while epithems are more liquid. Epithems are applied with cloths. When they are placed over the principal members, such as the heart, they should contain things that fortify and bear a <term>substine</term><note>original: "s'ustinu"; perhaps a protective or supportive substance.</note> of great virtue. Epithems should have a pleasant odor, which the vital spirits love.

<margin>or adhering</margin>
<margin>in others they warm the principal [organs]</margin>
<margin>or they retain</margin>
# Chapter 19. On Embrocations.
<margin>An embrocation is an infusion used in two ways: either to dissolve something or to stop the flow of humors.</margin>
**Embrocations** are medicines specifically for the head or other members to resolve [humors]. It is beneficial to change them according to the need. In those members which must be "embrocated" with heat or cold, if there are superfluities that descend, let the embrocation be made of warm things. Let them be made from iron-water <note>original: "aq' f'rū"; water in which hot iron had been quenched, believed to have medicinal properties.</note> and washed. And if the matter is hard, let them use steam or cold water.

# Chapter 20. On Bloodletting.
<margin>generation (?) in another, generation</margin>
**Phlebotomy** <note>original: "Flebotomia"; the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood.</note> is an evacuation of the vital spirit which removes a great quantity [of blood]. It is used when there is an increase of humors, especially when they are too warm or too thin. Note that bloodletting should be done for one of two reasons: either for those who are currently ill, when the sickness or the person is strong, or for those who fear future illness. One is bled either because of a "multitude" of blood or because of the "malice" <note>toxicity or corruption</note> of the blood, or both. Among those illnesses it helps are: gout <note>original: "podagre"</note>, <term>sciatica</term><note>original: "arte tice"</note>, or when one spits blood from a rupture in the lung, or for those who have too much blood. It also helps with epilepsy, apoplexy, and melancholy when there is a multitude of blood. It is used for those whose hemorrhoid flow is restricted, and for women whose menstrual blood is restricted. The colors of the blood demonstrate whether one should be bled due to the darkness of the humors, or their clarity, or their purity. And for the one who has an incision, it helps all heat-related weakness, and for these it is better to bleed from the hand.
